results.reason: The formula credited to Cachin is Anwar et al.'s restatement, which reverses the arguments of the (asymmetric) relative entropy. Cachin defines epsilon-security as D(P_C||P_S) <= epsilon, covertext first, stegotext second (checked in the revised text at cachin.com/cc/papers/stego.pdf, whose abstract is identical to IACR ePrint 2000/028, the map URL; no full text is cached). Proposition D.1 also does not recover epsilon-security as such: it shows the normalised gap equals 1 - TV(P0,P1) in that setting and, via Pinsker, is at least 1 - sqrt(epsilon/2) for an epsilon-secure system; the bound holds for either argument order.
evidence: Cachin, An Information-Theoretic Model for Steganography (revised 2004, cachin.com/cc/papers/stego.pdf), Definition 1: "a stegosystem is called ε-secure (against passive adversaries) if D(PC ‖ PS) ≤ ε."

anwar2026decision [P518]: "Let P0 denote the distribution of innocent covertexts and P1 the distribution of stegotexts. Cachin (2004) defines a steganographic system to be ε-secure if the Kullback-Leibler divergence between these distributions is bounded: DKL (P1 ∥P0 ) ≤ ε."

anwar2026decision [P522]: "Proposition D.1 (Classical Security as Special Case). Under the setup above, let TV = TV(P0 , P1 ) denote the total variation distance between covertext and stegotext distributions."; [P536]: "If the system is ε-secure, Pinsker’s inequality gives ... ∆̃steg(Z) = 1 − TV ≥ 1 − √(ε/2)"
results.replacement: The classical definition of [Cachin 1998](./#p=cachin1998information), $\varepsilon$-security $D(P_C\|P_S)\le\varepsilon$ between the covertext and stegotext distributions, is recovered as binary detection with an omnipotent Sentinel, where the normalised gap equals $1-\mathrm{TV}(P_0,P_1)$ and is at least $1-\sqrt{\varepsilon/2}$ for an $\varepsilon$-secure system (Proposition D.1).

results.reason: The sentence blends the two definitions and states each more weakly than its source. Kirchner et al.'s completeness requires the prover to always produce correct and accepted solutions, not only that the verifier accept correct ones. Kim & Lee's soundness is not limited to provers from the same model family: no incorrect proof at all may be accepted. Kim & Lee decouple correctness from checkability, so only Kirchner restricts the adversary to the model family.
evidence: kirchner2024proververifier [P65]: "Prover π from model family H is verifiable to verifier v on the data distribution P_XY if and only if the prover always generates correct and convincing solutions, and no adversarial / "sneaky" prover from the same model family H can fool the verifier into accepting incorrect solutions."

kim2026mitigating [P27]: "The prover is said to be checkable if there exists a verifier v such that the prover can always convince the verifier when its answer is correct, and there exists no adversarial proof that can trick the verifier into accepting an incorrect answer."
kim2026mitigating [P20]: "We propose decoupling correctness from the definition of checkability in Kirchner et al. (2024)."
results.replacement: In the catalogue, checkability is the completeness and soundness of a verifier: in [Kirchner et al. 2024](./#p=kirchner2024proververifier) the prover "always generates correct and convincing solutions" and no "sneaky" prover from the same model family can make the verifier accept an incorrect one, while [Kim & Lee 2026](./#p=kim2026mitigating) require only that the verifier accept the prover's correct answers but that "there exists no adversarial proof that can trick the verifier into accepting an incorrect answer".
